correctness.rationale: For tame separable f:E→P¹ of geometric degree three over F₂, tame Riemann–Hurwitz forces three geometric index-three ramification points and the geometric cover is cyclic C₃, so its deck automorphisms yield a Frobenius-stable order-three subgroup fixing a ramification point after translation to the elliptic origin. Ordinary j≠0 elliptic curves have only order-two origin-fixing geometric automorphisms, precluding such a subgroup. Among supersingular F₂ models E_{a,b}:y²+y=x³+a x+b, exact origin-fixing automorphism equations (u,r,s,t) with u³=1, s²=r, s=r²+a(1+u), t²+t=r³+a r classify all 24 over F₁₆; Frobenius acts coefficientwise. There are two Frobenius-stable C₃ subgroups when a=0 and none when a=1, independent of b. The five F₂ elliptic isomorphism classes have point counts 4,2,3,5,1, respectively, and the unique a=0 supersingular class has three points; the explicit degree-three function y realizes a tame cyclic quotient. Independent GF(16) exhaustive automorphism enumeration and point counts corroborate these finite data; the classification of all geometric automorphisms and Riemann–Hurwitz remain analytical premises.

originality.rationale: Kedlaya–Litt–Witaszek arXiv:2010.01130v2 proves that every smooth curve over a finite field admits some separable tame morphism, and Remark 8.4 explicitly supplies the geometrically cyclic cubic y for the supersingular a=0 form. That positive example is therefore not novel and is credited. The new claim is the degree-exact iff over F₂: only the three-rational-point elliptic curve has an everywhere-tame cubic, with a negative arithmetic-descent classification of the other four isomorphism types. Targeted arithmetical and Resultary searches did not find this exact criterion but novelty is best-of-knowledge.
residual_risks: Historical tables of tame degree-three maps or Galois point classifications of supersingular elliptic curves over F₂ might encode the same iff under different terminology.
Geometric-to-arithmetic descent requires the quotient conic to have a rational point; the chosen rational origin supplies it only after verifying an invariant subgroup and quotient map.
